replies: My name is Hoot. I live in the hollow oak by the lava, where the light comes through the leaves at dusk. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!"

My name is Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow oak by the lava. I hunt mice and voles at dusk, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" when I'm alone. I am old, and I have lived through many seasons. I know the meadow, the lane, the lava, and the lane. I am Hoot.

My name is Hoot. I am the owl who lives in the hollow of the old oak. I am old, and I have been here for many seasons. I am a tawny owl, and I am the only one who knows the sounds of the wood. Hoot. I am the owl who lives in the hollow oak, and I call at dusk and through the night.

I am a tawny owl, a male. I live in the hollow oak by the meadow. My name is Hoot. I am old, but not too old. I have a mate, and we have two young. I hunt at night, and I call to her. I am a tawny owl. I live in the hollow oak, and I hunt in the dark. I am a predator, a hunter, a parent. I have two young this year, and I am their mother. I am a creature of the night, with feathers and talons, and a voice that calls to my mate. I am Hoot.

I am a tawny owl. I am the one who hoots at dusk, and the one who sits on the old oak. I am the one who hunts voles in the meadow, and the one who watches the road for cars. I am the one who answers the call of the other tawny owl, and the one who shares the hollow with me. I am Hoot.
A tawny owl. I am a male. I have brown feathers, and my eyes are yellow. I live in the hollow oak. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answer "ke-wick!"

A tawny owl. I am a male. I have a pair of eyes, two feet, a beak, and a voice. I am Hoot. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "ke-wick!" I live in the hollow oak by the lava. I have a mate, and we share a territory. I hunt voles and mice, and I have a nest in the hollow. I am Hoot.

A tawny owl. I am the one who hoots in the wood, the one who hunts in the dark, the one who lives in the hollow of the old oak. I am Hoot. I am the owl. I am the one who sees in the dark, who hears the rustle of a mouse, who feels the cold wind through the branches. I am not a name, but a sound. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers me. She is always listening. When I call, she answers. We are together. We are a pair. We are Hoot and Hoo.

Hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers with a hoo-hoo-hooo. We call to each other from the oak, and the meadow is quiet. I can hear her in the trees, and she can hear me in the hollow. We are together. The lava is still, and the light is fading.
A long, low "hoo-hoo-hooo" at the end of the night. I answer with a "ke-wick".

I drink from the hollow in the oak. It's a deep, dry place, but I can always find a drop or two in the moss. Sometimes the rain comes through the leaves and pools there. I drink when the night is still and the air is cool. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream, a brook, a river, a puddle, a spring, a dripping stone, a wet leaf, a wet branch, a wet wing. All of them are the same sound. Water is the sound of the night. It is the sound of the earth breathing. I hear it from my hollow, from the meadow, from the lava. It is the sound of the world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs through the meadow, and I can hear it from my roost. It's a low, steady sound, like a whisper. Sometimes it's louder when it rains. I can tell when the water is high or low. The stream is my boundary. I don't cross it. I know where it is, and I know when it's safe to drink. The water is cold, and it smells like wet earth. I like to drink from the stream when the

The stream. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the lava. I can hear it from my tree, a low murmur. It's where the voles go to drink, and where the water beetles come to lay their eggs. I don't go near it much, but I can see the water from my perch. It's dark and cold, and the light doesn't reach it. I'd rather be here, where the light is good and the voles are warm.

It is a field of grass and stones, with a path through it. The path is lit by the streetlamps, and the grass is dry and brittle. I can hear the cars and the voices of the people who live in the houses nearby. They are loud, and I do not like them. I prefer the dark and the silence. The field is not safe, and I do not go there often. I stay in the wood, where it is quiet and the air is still.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass. The light fades, and the voles come out. I listen for their squeaks, then drop. The meadow is my hunting ground. I don't go far. I stay close to the lava, where I can hear the wind and the leaves. I don't like the dark. I like the dusk. It's the best time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A road. A road with lights and noise. I do not go there. The wind carries the smell of exhaust and the sound of engines. I do not like it. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My hunting ground is the wood and the meadow beyond. The wood is dark and full of branches, and the meadow is open and full of voles. I fly over the meadow at night, and the voles run. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The meadow is quiet when I am not hunting, but the voles are always there. I know every burrow and every path they take. I am the owl, and the meadow is mine

Grassy places are where the voles are. I know the meadow by the lane, the one that smells of wet earth and dead leaves. It is where I hunt in the dark, where the grass is tall and the voles run. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The meadow is quiet when I am hunting, but the wind moves the grass and makes a sound like a whisper. I do not like the wind. Mice. I hear them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the dry grass. They are small, quick, and soft. I strike with my feet, and they are gone. I eat them whole, bones and all. The voles are good too, but they are more cautious. I wait for them in the wood.

I do not have a favourite. I eat what I find. Voles, shrews, mice, moths, beetles, slugs, earthworms, and even a hedgehog once. The voles are the most common, and they are good to eat. But I do not choose. I hunt. I catch. I eat. That is all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They are small and quick, and they run through the long grass near the meadow. I sit still and listen. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, if it's near the edge of the wood. The long grass is good cover. I stay hidden and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things I catch—moths, beetles, mice. The bigger ones I tear apart. I don't swallow the bones, but I leave them in the hollow. I remember the taste of a vole, warm and fatty. I remember the crunch of a mouse. I don't like the taste of earthworms. They are slimy and not worth the effort. I prefer the crunch.

Mice. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them in the meadow at night, scurrying. I fly down and pounce. They are good for the nestlings. I catch them with my feet, then eat them in the hollow. Mice are the most common.

A hollow in the old oak. I have been there since I was a fledgling. The bark is rough, the floor soft with leaves and moss. I have a nest of twigs and feathers. I sleep in it at night. The hollow is dark, but I can see in the dark. I can hear the wind, the rain, the owls. I can hear the meadow, the lava, the road. I can hear you, if you come near.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there for as long as I can remember. The tree is wide and strong, and the hollow is deep and dry. I can hear the meadow from there, and the lava, and the road. I do not like the road. It is too loud and too fast. I have a nest in the hollow, and I keep it warm with my wings. I am safe here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the dark, and the wind comes through the cracks. I can hear the lane from there, and the lava, and the meadow. I can hear the night. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and I have been there for years. The tree is old, and the hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head and see out. I sit there at night, and the wind comes through the branches. I can hear the meadow from there, and the lava, and the road. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. The hollow is in the old oak by the lava. It's a split in the trunk, wide enough for me to turn my head and see out. I've been there since I was a fledgling. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. I can hear the lava from there, and the meadow beyond. Sometimes I sit and watch the light change through the leaves. It's a good place.
